what: An idempotency store remembers which requests or jobs already ran, keyed by a unique idempotency key. When a retry or duplicate arrives, it returns the saved result instead of doing the work twice.
like: Like a cloakroom ticket: show the same ticket twice and you get the same coat back, not a second coat.
why: Networks and queues retry, so the same request often arrives more than once
Stops double charges, double emails and double-counted results
Lets clients retry freely after a timeout without fear

nodes.t: Client or worker|sends key with request

steps.d: The client makes a unique key (often a random UUID) and sends it with the request, for example in an Idempotency-Key header. A retry reuses the same key.
Queues deliver at least once, so a crash or timeout can hand the same job over again. The service treats every arrival as maybe a repeat.
The service checks the store. Key found with a finished result? Return that saved result straight away, without doing the work again.
New key: insert a row with status running under a unique constraint. Only one insert can win, so two copies arriving together cannot both start.
Run the real action, then store the response next to the key and mark it done. Ideally the work and the key commit in one transaction.
Keys are kept for a retention window, then removed by a TTL job so the store does not grow forever.

choices.d: Client-made UUIDs suit API calls. For jobs, build a natural key from the business facts, like project + prompt + engine + day + run, so any retry produces the same key.
Same database as the data lets key and work commit together. Redis SET with NX and a TTL is fast but can lose keys on failover.
Keep keys longer than your longest retry period, including queue redelivery and manual replays. Stripe uses about 24 hours.
Return the saved response, even a saved error, so the client sees one consistent answer. Reject a reused key whose body differs.
If the key is still running, answer 409 or ask the caller to retry later. Give the lock a timeout so a crashed worker does not block it forever.

instead.why: A unique constraint plus upsert can be the whole idempotency store
SET NX with TTL for quick, short-lived dedupe
Idempotent producer and transactions dedupe inside the log itself
Parks jobs that keep failing so retries stop piling up

breaks.d: Two copies both read 'no key' and both run the work.
breaks.see: Duplicate rows or double charges that arrived within milliseconds
breaks.fix: Claim the key with an atomic insert under a unique constraint, not a read first

breaks.d: A late retry or replay arrives after the TTL, so the work runs again.
breaks.see: Duplicates that line up with old redeliveries or backfills
breaks.fix: Retention longer than the max retry window, or a natural key stored with the data

breaks.d: A worker crashes after claiming the key, so every retry sees running.
breaks.see: Keys stuck in running status, jobs never completing
breaks.fix: Lock timeout or lease, then let a retry reclaim it

breaks.d: The key and the real write are stored separately and only one commits.
breaks.see: Saved success with no matching data, or data with no key
breaks.fix: Commit key and work in one transaction, or make the write itself an upsert

breaks.d: A client bug reuses a key for a new request.
breaks.see: Users get an old answer for a new request
breaks.fix: Store a hash of the body and reject mismatches

say: Delivery is at-least-once, so I assume every job can arrive twice and make the handler idempotent.
Each AI-engine check gets a natural key of project, prompt, engine, day and run number, and the result row has a unique constraint on it, so I write with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.
A retried job then becomes a no-op instead of counting a citation twice, which keeps visibility scores honest.
True exactly-once is really effectively-once: at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing.

followups.a: Across a network, not as pure delivery. Systems give effectively-once: retry until acknowledged, then dedupe. Kafka does this with producer IDs and sequence numbers per partition, plus transactions for writes across partitions.

followups.q: Where does the in-progress state live?
followups.a: In the same row as the key: status running, done or failed, plus a lock expiry. A retry seeing running waits or gets a 409; one seeing done gets the saved result.
UUIDs work when the client keeps the key across its own retries. For scheduled jobs a natural key is better, because a rerun from scratch still builds the same key.

followups.q: How do you clean up keys?
followups.a: Give each key a created time and delete or expire rows older than the retention window, with a TTL index or a periodic job. Keep it longer than any retry path.

today: Kafka producers have been idempotent by default since Kafka 3.0, using a producer ID and per-partition sequence numbers so brokers drop duplicate batches.

check.q: Your queue promises at-least-once delivery. What must the consumer assume?
check.a: Any message may arrive more than once
check.why: At-least-once means retries until acknowledged, so repeats are expected.

check.q: Two copies of a job arrive at the same moment. What stops both running?
check.a: An atomic insert of the key under a unique constraint
d: Reading the key first, then writing
check.why: Only one insert can win the constraint; read-then-write leaves a gap both can slip through.

check.q: Which key best dedupes a daily AI-engine visibility check?
d: A new random UUID per attempt
check.why: A natural key is rebuilt the same way on every retry, so duplicates collide.

check.q: A Stripe retry reuses a key whose first try returned a 500. What comes back?
check.why: Stripe saves the first result for the key, errors included, once the endpoint started running.
